stem: A 27-year-old female with a history of oral contraceptive use is found to have an incidental liver lesion on imaging. She discontinues oral contraceptives, and after 6 months, follow-up imaging shows that the lesion has not regressed. What is the most appropriate next step?
srcNote: Source note (Final 437 F Q18 (p. 83)): The related recall describes a 4x4 cm adenoma in a patient with no history of contraceptive medication. It gives A. Liver resection. Answer: A, answer is liver resection cause pts adenoma is not secondary to OCP use, if OCP you stop and observe for 6-12m no improvement -> Do surgery.
expl: Suspected hepatic adenoma in an OCP user: stop OCPs and re-image; if it doesn't regress (or is >5 cm, grows, bleeds, or in a man) → resection (risk of rupture and malignant change).

why.A: Already observed; persistent lesion needs resection.

stem: A 35-year-old woman undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for nonspecific abdominal discomfort. Imaging reveals a well-circumscribed, hypervascular liver lesion with a central stellate scar on CR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A well-circumscribed hypervascular lesion with a central stellate scar = focal nodular hyperplasia.

stem: A 48-year-old patient undergoes a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the liver. Imaging reveals a hepatic lesion with peripheral nodular enhancement and gradual centripetal fill-in on delayed phases. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in on delayed phases is pathognomonic of haemangioma.

stem: Female had trauma did CT found incidental liver mass , the mass had arterial enhancement and patient taking oral contraceptives what is the best management? Source recall answer: Stop contraceptives and followup imaging in 6 months Incomplete recall: the source provides an answer phrase without a choice set.
expl: An arterially enhancing incidental liver mass in a woman on OCPs is most likely a hepatic adenoma (oestrogen-dependent).
ansText: Stop the oral contraceptive and repeat imaging in about 6 months (source answer) — a presumed hepatic adenoma often regresses; persistence, growth or >5 cm → resection.

stem: 58 year old male known case of hepatitis C and liver cirrhosis. Presents with US results of focal liver 2cm lesion. Triphasic CT showed liver lesion in segment 3 with early arterial enhancement and early “washout”. What is the diagnosis?
expl: In a cirrhotic liver, a lesion with arterial hyperenhancement and portal/delayed washout is diagnostic of HCC (no biopsy needed).

why.C: Rare in cirrhotic livers; rim enhancement.

stem: A 30-year-old female diagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma 4 cm in size with child's B cirrhosis. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

opts.t: Hepatic resection with 2 cm margin of normal live

srcNote: (Transplant surgery) Source note (Midterm 436 A Q31): Milan criteria: Cirrhosis + child B + single nodule size <5cm = transplant Milan criteria (a set of criteria used to assess HCC patients for transplant) 1 tumor measuring ≥ 2 cm and ≤ 5 cm OR 2-3 tumors measuring ≥ 1 cm and ≤ 3 cm
expl: Milan criteria: single tumor ≤5 cm or up to 3 tumors ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion. Child B cirrhosis + 4 cm HCC → transplant.

why.A: Resection is unsafe in Child B cirrhosis.
why.C: RFA is for small tumors (<3 cm) and doesn't treat cirrhosis.

stem: A 35 Year old man underwent CT scan abdomen with incidental finding of 3-cm lesion in the periphery of the left lobe of the liver. The lesion enhances on the arterial phase of the CT and has central scar suggestive of focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH). Which of the following is the best management option for this patient?
expl: FNH is benign with no malignant potential and rarely bleeds → no treatment when typical and asymptomatic.

stem: Which one of the following structures does not form the portal triad?
expl: The portal triad (in the hepatoduodenal ligament/portal tracts) = portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct. Hepatic veins drain separately into the IVC.

stem: Patient comes with cyst in investigations. CT shows a singular mass in segment 8 (?). Which of the following cyst can look like a solid mass on CT of the liver?
srcNote: not sure (Liver masses) Unanswered source question: the original key states "not sure" without identifying an option.
expl: No key in the source ("not sure"). A degenerated/calcified (inactive) hydatid cyst or one full of daughter cysts and matrix can look solid on CT. Biloma and cystadenoma look cystic; metastasis is solid, not a cyst.

stem: A 48-year-old female, heavy smoker, was admitted to the hospital for investigation of liver cirrhosis. During her workup, she was found to have a hepatocellular carcinoma in her liver. She had positive tests for HBV and HCV. She is known to take Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) as a treatment for menopause Which of the following has the weakest association with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)?
expl: Among her risks, HBV and HCV are strong HCC risks and smoking is a recognised modest risk; oestrogen exposure (OCP/HRT) is associated with hepatic adenoma, and has the weakest link to HCC. (Source: "Ans B".)

stem: A 32-year-old man presented with right upper quadrant pain and fever for 2 weeks. CT scan the abdomen demonstrated a non-rim enhancing fluid collection in the periphery of the right lobe of the liver. The patient's serology is positive for antibodies to Entameba histolytica Which of the following is the best initial management option for this patient?

opts.t: Percutaneous drainage of the fluid collection

srcNote: Source note (Final Year not stated Q16 (p. 260)): The related recall gives A. Metronidazole. Answer: a.
expl: Amoebic liver abscess → metronidazole (then a luminal agent); drainage only for failure, impending rupture or left-lobe abscess.

stem: Which of the following is the most serious complication of hydatid disease of the liver?
expl: Rupture/spillage of hydatid fluid can cause fatal anaphylaxis — the most serious complication (hence hypertonic saline/scolicidal precautions at surgery).

why.B: Secondary infection — serious but less so.
why.D: From rupture into bile ducts — less serious.

stem: Egyptian male, had history of bilharziasis:
srcNote: ??? incomplete Q Incomplete and unanswered recall: only one choice is supplied, and the source gives "???" as the answer.
expl: The recall is incomplete — learn bilharziasis → pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension, varices, and HCC risk via HCV co-infection.
ansText: Hepatocellular carcinoma risk (the only recalled option). Schistosoma mansoni causes periportal (pipe-stem) fibrosis → pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension with preserved liver function; in Egypt it is strongly linked to HCV (spread by mass parenteral antischistosomal therapy), so HCC risk is high.

stem: All liver cyst except “not complete Q”
srcNote: Incomplete recall: the source lists "Metastatic" and "colon cancer" separately and supplies no complete choice set.
expl: The question is incomplete; the keyed fact is that metastases are the commonest malignant liver lesions (and are not true cysts).

why.B: Colon cancer is a common source of liver metastases.

opts.t: is most commonly in Bifurcation of hepatic duct

srcNote: Incomplete recall: only one choice is supplied in the source.
expl: Cholangiocarcinoma most commonly arises at the hepatic duct bifurcation (hilar/Klatskin tumor, ~60%).

stem: Paraneoplastic syndrome for hepatocellular carcinoma cause all except
srcNote: , paraneoplastic syndromes (PNS) which have been associated with HCC include hypercholesterolemia, hypercalcemia, erythrocytosis, hypoglycemia, demyelinating disease, pemphigus, polyarthritis, encephalomyelitis, and thrombocytosis
expl: HCC paraneoplastic syndromes include hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypercholesterolemia and erythrocytosis — not hyperglycemia. ("Hypocholesterolemia" in option D is also not typical; the keyed answer is A.)

stem: All can predispose to hepatocellular cancer except
srcNote: , it’s the least risk The original key and the accompanying source risk-factor image are reproduced as supplied.
expl: Cirrhosis and hepatitis B/C cause HCC. Hepatitis A does not cause chronic liver disease — yet the source keyed smoking as "the least risk". Know both facts.

why.C: Hepatitis A doesn't cause chronic infection or HCC.

stem: Women diagnosed with liver abscess in the right lobe sample of the abscess was taken and showed streptococcus faecalis. Which of the following is the root of transmission?
expl: Pyogenic liver abscess with a gut organism (Enterococcus/Streptococcus faecalis) reaches the liver through the portal vein (pylephlebitis from appendicitis/diverticulitis). Biliary route is the most common overall (cholangitis).

why.C: Ascending cholangitis — most common overall, but the organism points to portal spread.

stem: Patient known case of hepatitis B induced cirrhosis developed jaundice over 3 months and weight loss. CT done showed hypervascular mass with central necrosis. Which of the following is the best to confirm the diagnosis?
srcNote: Incomplete choice set: only three options are provided in the source.
expl: In HBV cirrhosis with a hypervascular mass, a markedly raised α-fetoprotein supports HCC (CEA → colorectal; CA 19-9 → pancreas/cholangiocarcinoma).
